title: Fossil Fuel Phase-Out
scope: Restricting fossil fuel production rather than only curbing demand.
primary_image_prompt:
A minimalist flat vector-style icon illustration, in a clean editorial line-art style: A working extraction site read as one landscape: a large pumpjack, the dominant focal mass, stands right of center on a softly rising curved ridge, its nodding beam tilted down and its counterweight overlapping the tower behind it; a tall lattice drilling derrick sits just behind and to the left, partly hidden by the pumpjack's beam; a thick pipeline runs the full width of the frame as the connective element, entering at the left edge, bending over a low saddle in the ground curve and passing behind the pumpjack's base before leaving at the right edge; two squat cylindrical storage tanks of medium size cluster at the lower left, one overlapping the other and both overlapping the pipeline; a small capped wellhead with a round valve wheel stands in the near foreground at lower right, the smallest element; the ground is a single long shallow curve with a second fainter curve behind it suggesting distance, and a short band of layered strata lines reads under the ridge at the left.

Composition: one dominant focal mass with smaller supporting elements at clearly different scales (big, medium, small); at least one element overlaps another so the scene has depth; the ground is a gentle curve, never a flat line; one connective element runs across the frame to tie the pieces together. A single coherent scene, not a row of separate objects. Centered with generous, even padding.

Style: monoline line art with ONE uniform stroke weight on every element, including the thinnest wisps and lines. Rounded line caps and corners. Confident, slightly bold strokes so it stays legible when small. No fussy internal detail.

Color: a single hue, two tones only. Draw all lines in solid #3f9a6a, and give every major mass a clearly visible soft fill of the same hue at about 15-18% opacity, so the duotone is obviously present rather than white interiors. No other colors, no gradients, no shadows, no 3D, no texture.

Important: NO border, NO frame, NO box or outline around the scene, just the illustration on a plain white background. No text, letters, or numbers. No human figures or faces. Calm, neutral, editorial mood: show the subject plainly, neither celebrating nor warning. Also avoid: no smokestacks belching black smoke, no flames or gas flares, no skull or crossbones, no dying planet or melting globe, no protest signs or banners, no wind turbines or solar panels, no clock or hourglass, no arrows, no crossed-out or prohibition symbols, no money or coins, no text or numbers, no people or hands, no faces, no frame or border, no vignette, no second color, no drop shadows.

overview.summary: Whether governments should restrict the extraction of coal, oil and gas itself, rather than only the demand that burns it.
overview.scope_covered: Refusing new exploration licenses and leases, dated end points for national output, public finance and export credit for extraction, producer subsidies, and the proposal for a binding treaty that allocates production declines between countries.
overview.scope_excluded: How fast the whole economy should decarbonize, carbon dioxide removal and geoengineering. Consumer-side instruments such as carbon pricing or vehicle mandates appear only where they bear on the supply question.
overview.why_now: In April 2026, Colombia and the Netherlands hosted the first intergovernmental conference on leaving fossil fuels, in Santa Marta. Fifty-seven states came. It set up voluntary workstreams, not a treaty; the first helps countries draft national roadmaps away from fossil fuels.

stats.label: Planned 2030 output above a 1.5 °C path
stats.note: Governments’ own production plans for 2030 add up to about 120 percent more coal, oil and gas than a median 1.5 °C pathway allows, with coal furthest out of line.
stats.detail: This is the only regular global accounting of what governments plan to extract, as opposed to what they pledge to emit. The 2025 edition profiles 20 major producer countries that together account for over 82 percent of world production. The shortfall has widened since the 2023 edition, which put combined 2030 plans at 110 percent above a 1.5 °C path. Government plans also exceed what those same governments’ own climate pledges imply, by 35 percent in 2030 and 141 percent in 2050; planned coal output to 2035 and planned gas output to 2050 are both higher than they were in the 2023 assessment; and 11 of the 20 profiled countries have raised near-term plans for at least one fuel since then. The report notes that several governments promote gas as a transition fuel without any explicit plan to transition away from it.
stats.source_label: Production Gap Report 2025 (SEI, Climate Analytics, IISD)

stats.label: Fossil CO2 emissions, world
stats.note: Burning coal, oil and gas released a record 38.1 billion tonnes of CO2 in 2025, with all three fuels above their 2024 levels.
stats.detail: The Global Carbon Budget is the annual international stocktake of carbon flows, produced by a consortium of more than a hundred research institutions. Its 2025 edition records the eleventh consecutive year in which the world has not reduced emissions from fossil fuels: coal rose 0.8 percent on 2024, oil 1.0 percent and gas 1.3 percent. Land-use change adds a further 4.1 billion tonnes, for total human emissions of about 42.2 billion tonnes. Atmospheric CO2 is projected at 425.7 parts per million for 2025, about 52 percent above the pre-industrial level. Regional projections for the year show emissions rising in China, India, the United States and the European Union, and falling in Japan. That three decades of demand-side climate policy have coincided with this record is the starting point for arguments on every side of this page.
stats.source_label: Global Carbon Budget 2025, Global Carbon Project

stats.label: Fossil fuel share of world energy supply
stats.note: Fossil fuels supplied 86.2 percent of world energy in 2025, about four percentage points below their 1990 share.
stats.detail: Total energy supply roughly doubled over the same thirty-five years, so the absolute quantity of coal, oil and gas burned has risen throughout, even as the share slipped. The accounting basis matters and changes the number: this series counts non-fossil electricity at its input heat requirement and reports total energy supply, while direct-equivalent accounting or counting only final energy gives different percentages. The Energy Institute’s 2026 review also reports that total energy supply passed 600 exajoules in 2025, up 1.7 percent, and that renewables were the largest single source of that growth for the first time outside a recession. Both fossil and non-fossil supply grew.
stats.source_label: Energy Institute Statistical Review of World Energy, via Our World in Data

stats.label: Remaining carbon budget for 1.5 °C
stats.note: About 170 billion tonnes of CO2 remain from the start of 2026 for a 50 percent chance of holding warming to 1.5 °C — roughly four years at 2025 emission rates.
stats.detail: A carbon budget is a statistical quantity, not a cliff: it is the cumulative CO2 that can still be released for a stated probability of staying under a stated temperature, and it moves as each year’s emissions are subtracted and as estimates of how strongly the climate responds are revised. Pierre Friedlingstein of the University of Exeter, who led the 2025 assessment, said on publication that with emissions still rising, keeping warming below 1.5 °C is no longer plausible. The relevance to extraction policy is arithmetic rather than rhetorical: the budget is far smaller than the emissions already locked in by fossil fuel infrastructure that exists or is being built, which is the premise behind the case for restricting supply rather than waiting for demand to fall.
stats.source_label: Global Carbon Budget 2025, Global Carbon Project

stats.label: Government revenue from fossil fuels, dependent economies
stats.note: Across 40 heavily fossil-fuel-dependent countries, extraction revenue averages 38.6 percent of all government income.
stats.detail: In the same group of countries fossil fuels make up 61.2 percent of exports, and resource rents average 14.3 percent of GDP, with a median of 11.1 percent. This is the distributional core of the dispute and the reason just transition language appears in every supply-side proposal: a schedule set by climate arithmetic alone would ask states whose public budgets are two-fifths funded by hydrocarbons to give that up without a replacement source of income, and most of them are not wealthy. The remedies on offer run from sequencing that puts wealthy producers first, to debt-for-climate swaps, to direct compensation funds. As of 2026, none has been financed at anything approaching the scale of the revenue involved.
stats.source_label: UNDP, Global Decarbonization in Fossil Fuel Export-Dependent Economies

stats.label: CO2 committed by extraction already built
stats.note: Oil and gas fields and coal mines already producing or under construction would emit 936 billion tonnes of CO2 if each were run to the end of its life.
stats.detail: This was the first bottom-up accounting of committed emissions from extraction infrastructure specifically, rather than from power plants and factories. Coal accounts for 47 percent of the total, oil 35 percent and gas 18 percent. Measured against the budgets the study used, the figure is 60 percent larger than a 1.5 °C budget of 580 billion tonnes and 95 percent of a 2 °C budget of 980 billion tonnes; both of those IPCC values have since been revised downward, which makes the overshoot larger rather than smaller. The authors conclude that staying within a 1.5 °C budget at even odds requires leaving almost 40 percent of already developed reserves unextracted — something no policy of refusing new licenses achieves on its own.
stats.source_label: Trout et al., Environmental Research Letters

stats.label: World consumption change per barrel of production withheld
stats.note: In the most-cited model, withholding a barrel of production removes about 0.6 barrels from world consumption; the authors’ own sensitivity range runs from 0.08 to 0.78.
stats.detail: The study was written about the Keystone XL pipeline and modeled what adding capacity does to a market with given supply and demand elasticities; read in reverse, it gives the figure most often quoted for how much of a production cut survives rather than being made up elsewhere. The spread comes from the elasticity assumptions, which differ by fuel, by region and by time horizon. Two cautions travel with it. The result is specific to oil: coal and gas are traded less globally and priced more regionally, and as of 2026 no comparable central estimate has been published for them. And with the policy untried at scale as of 2026, there is no observed case against which the model can be checked.
stats.source_label: Erickson and Lazarus, Nature Climate Change

stats.label: Top five countries’ share of world fossil production
stats.note: China, the United States, Russia, Saudi Arabia and Canada together produce just over half of the world’s coal, oil and gas.
stats.detail: The combined share was calculated by summing Our World in Data’s oil, gas and coal production series, measured in terawatt-hours, for 2025: China 21.4 percent, the United States 16.4, Russia 10.0, Saudi Arabia 5.2 and Canada 4.0, with the top ten countries at 73.5 percent. Concentration varies by fuel, with the three largest producers holding 41.5 percent of oil, 46.4 percent of gas and 71.2 percent of coal. As of 2026, none of the four largest has joined any coalition committed to restricting production. That same concentration is read in opposite directions on this page, as the reason a production agreement among a few parties could cover most of world supply, and as the reason restriction by anyone else changes little.
stats.source_label: Energy Institute Statistical Review, via Our World in Data; shares summed by Ideya

stats.label: Reserves that must stay unextracted by 2050
stats.note: For a 50 percent chance of 1.5 °C, 89 percent of coal reserves and roughly three-fifths of gas and oil reserves must stay in the ground to 2050.
stats.detail: This University College London study is the paper most often cited as the quantitative foundation of the phrase keep it in the ground, and the same model has oil and gas production falling about 3 percent a year globally to mid-century. Its authors stress that the shares are likely underestimates, because they assume only a coin-flip chance of 1.5 °C and substantial deployment of carbon dioxide removal. The regional detail is what makes it politically explosive: Middle East oil output halving within thirty years, United States gas production down 90 percent, 99 percent of unconventional oil left alone and no production at all from currently undeveloped Arctic fields. Which reserves count as unextractable depends on cost, so the model spares the cheapest producers and strands the most expensive — an outcome several producer governments dispute as an equity matter rather than a scientific one.
stats.source_label: Welsby, Price, Pye and Ekins, Nature

stats.label: Fall in oil output if upstream investment stopped
stats.note: If capital spending on existing oil and gas fields stopped, world oil output would fall about 8 percent a year and gas about 9 percent, the IEA estimates.
stats.detail: The agency built this from field-by-field production records for roughly 15,000 oil and gas fields. In volume the losses are about 5.5 million barrels of oil a day each year, more than Brazil and Norway produce combined, and about 270 billion cubic meters of gas, roughly all of Africa’s gas output at the time of the 2025 report. With investment continuing, observed post-peak decline is gentler: 5.6 percent a year for conventional oil and 6.8 percent for conventional gas. The report also finds that nearly 90 percent of upstream investment since 2019 has gone to offsetting decline rather than to growth. Both sides of this argument cite the same numbers — as evidence that cutting investment causes shortage, or as evidence that simply declining to issue new licenses delivers a steep decline on its own.
stats.source_label: IEA, The Implications of Oil and Gas Field Decline Rates

stats.label: Government support for fossil fuels
stats.note: Governments spent USD 0.92 trillion supporting fossil fuels in 2024 on the OECD’s fiscal measure; the IMF, also counting unpriced pollution and climate costs, puts the total at USD 7.4 trillion.
stats.detail: The two headline numbers are not alternatives for the same thing. The OECD counts money that actually moves or taxes actually foregone, across 49 economies, and records a fall from USD 1.03 trillion in 2023, with 84.2 percent of the support going to consumption rather than production. The IMF, covering 170 countries, splits its figure into USD 725 billion of explicit subsidies and USD 6.7 trillion of implicit ones, mainly the gap between what fuels cost and what they would cost if priced to cover pollution, congestion and accidents. That most support flows to consumption complicates the supply-side framing, because removing it raises prices for households. The IMF paper estimates that removing explicit subsidies alone would cut CO2 about 6 percent below baseline in 2035, and that for every dollar spent on them the poorest fifth of households receive about 8 cents.
stats.source_label: OECD Inventory of Support Measures for Fossil Fuels 2025

stats.label: New coal-fired capacity commissioned
stats.note: The world brought 97.4 gigawatts of new coal capacity online in 2025, the second-highest annual total on record, even as coal-fired generation fell.
stats.detail: The global coal fleet grew 3.5 percent over the year while the electricity it generated fell 0.6 percent. China commissioned about 78 gigawatts, its highest in a decade, and 95 percent of the coal capacity under construction worldwide in 2025 was in China or India. Global Energy Monitor reads the divergence as plants being built for grid reliability and peak demand while record wind and solar additions take the energy. Which reading proves right matters a great deal: if the new plants run at low capacity factors they are expensive insurance, and if they run at high ones they lock in emissions for decades.
stats.source_label: Global Energy Monitor, Boom and Bust Coal 2026

stats.label: World Court judges holding climate inaction can be wrongful
stats.note: All 15 judges of the world court held in July 2025 that a state’s failure to act on climate, including production, licensing and subsidies, may be an internationally wrongful act.
stats.detail: The opinion was requested by the UN General Assembly in March 2023 on an initiative led by Vanuatu and backed by 105 co-sponsoring states, and unanimity is rare in the Court’s history. An advisory opinion is not binding in itself; its force comes from being the authoritative statement of what existing obligations mean, which domestic courts, arbitral tribunals and treaty negotiators then draw on. Paragraph 427 is the passage that matters here, because it names production, licensing and subsidies specifically, moving extraction policy from a matter of sovereign discretion to one on which a state can be found in breach. A follow-up General Assembly resolution to put the opinion into practice, again led by Vanuatu, drew opposition from the United States, Russia and Saudi Arabia.
stats.source_label: International Court of Justice, Obligations of States in Respect of Climate Change

stats.label: Annulled award against Italy for refusing an oil concession
stats.note: A 2022 arbitral award ordered Italy to pay Rockhopper EUR 190 million for refusing an oil concession; an ICSID committee annulled it in June 2025.
stats.detail: Investor-state arbitration is the main legal obstacle a government faces when it restricts extraction after investors have committed capital, because treaties such as the Energy Charter Treaty allow claims for lost future profit, not only for money spent: Rockhopper had invested EUR 29.2 million. The committee annulled the award unanimously because one arbitrator had not disclosed a decades-old criminal conviction, not on the merits. The European Union and Euratom withdrew from the Energy Charter Treaty on 28 June 2025, but its sunset clause protects investments made before exit for twenty years, to 2045, unless the remaining parties agree otherwise. A separate claim by RWE sought EUR 1.4 billion from the Netherlands over its 2030 coal phase-out; RWE withdrew it in 2023. Investors and some legal scholars argue these protections are what make long-horizon energy investment possible in weak-rule-of-law jurisdictions at all, and that stripping them raises the cost of capital for clean energy too.
stats.source_label: Rockhopper Exploration plc v. Italian Republic, case record at Climate Case Chart

stats.label: Upstream oil and gas value at risk of stranding
stats.note: Shifting market expectations to match governments’ stated climate policies would strand about USD 1.4 trillion of upstream oil and gas value, on one modeled scenario.
stats.detail: The study’s contribution is tracing where the loss lands rather than estimating its size. Following 43,439 assets through a network of 1.8 million companies, it finds about USD 690 billion of the loss reaching financial markets — which the authors compare to the mispricing behind the 2007-08 crisis — and about USD 484 billion owned directly by governments. Most of the remainder ends with pension funds and individual shareholders in wealthy countries, amounting to a net transfer of more than 15 percent of global stranded-asset risk to investors based in OECD economies. That is also the basis of the financial-stability case central banks make: an abrupt repricing is more damaging than a scheduled one, which argues for announcing a phase-out path rather than for avoiding one. The figure is a present value under one set of assumptions, not a forecast of realized losses.
stats.source_label: Semieniuk et al., Nature Climate Change

stats.label: Premature deaths from fossil fuel air pollution
stats.note: One modeling study attributes 8.7 million premature deaths a year to fine particles from fossil fuels; others are far lower, and its 95 percent confidence interval runs from below zero to 14 million.
stats.detail: The figure comes from Vohra and colleagues, using 2018 exposure data in the GEOS-Chem atmospheric model, and splits as 3.9 million deaths in China and 2.5 million in India. It sits at the high end of the literature: the World Health Organization attributes about 4.2 million deaths a year to ambient fine-particle pollution from all sources, and other peer-reviewed estimates of the fossil fuel share come closer to 3.6 million. Estimates vary this widely because they depend on the assumed relationship between exposure and mortality. The reason the number belongs on this page at all is that it is the main non-climate argument for restricting supply: the health gains are local and immediate and accrue to the country doing the restricting, which changes the calculation about production moving elsewhere.

stats.label: Want their country to move quickly off fossil fuels
stats.note: Asked whether their country should transition quickly from fossil fuels to renewables, 72 percent worldwide said yes, and 7 percent said it should not transition at all.
stats.detail: The Peoples’ Climate Vote is the largest survey of public opinion on climate conducted anywhere, with more than 73,000 respondents across 77 countries representing about 87 percent of world population. It found majorities for a quick transition in each of the ten largest producers of oil, coal or gas, from 54 percent in the United States to 89 percent in Nigeria. Two limits travel with the number. The question asks about the speed of the energy transition in the respondent’s own country, not about restricting extraction, which is a narrower and less familiar proposal. And it attaches no price: surveys that specify a cost to the respondent consistently return lower support.
stats.source_label: UNDP and University of Oxford, Peoples’ Climate Vote 2024

questions.text: Does restricting production in one country cut global emissions, or just move extraction elsewhere?
questions.why: As of 2026, no large producer has held back output for climate reasons, so there is no clean test. The answer turns on assumed supply and demand elasticities, and the published range is wide enough to support opposite conclusions.
questions.detail:
Those who expect real reductions argue that a pass-through of roughly 60 percent is not leakage in the dismissive sense: it compares well with demand-side instruments, which leak too, through industrial competitiveness and through the way prices rebound when one country consumes less. Leakage should also be lower for coal and gas, which are bulkier to ship and often burned near where they are dug or piped. Beyond the arithmetic, they argue the models miss the main mechanism. Refusing a license is a visible, durable, legally binding act that shifts expectations about future demand, and expectations are what drive capital allocation. A carbon tax can be repealed in a budget; a canceled field is a decade of capital that never moved.

Those who expect displacement read the low end of the same range as the relevant one, because markets with spare capacity behave differently. OPEC+ holds several million barrels a day idle precisely so it can fill gaps, and when a high-cost producer withdraws, a low-cost one typically takes the space. Ecuador is the case they point to: a national referendum in 2023 voted 59 percent to stop extraction in the Yasuní ITT block, and Human Rights Watch reported in August 2025 that extraction was continuing, with only a handful of the block’s roughly 240 wells closed. On this reading the restricting country has transferred the revenue, not the emissions.

questions.text: Should governments stop issuing new extraction licenses now, or only once replacement supply is in place?
questions.why: Both sides accept that licensing has to end eventually. They disagree about which risk is worse, locking in a new thirty-year asset or opening a supply gap, and the two risks land on different people.
questions.detail:
The case for stopping now starts with the International Energy Agency’s net-zero scenario, which concludes that no new long-lead-time upstream oil and gas projects are needed, nor new coal mines, mine extensions or unabated coal plants. Fields take years to sanction and decades to produce, so a license granted in the mid-2020s sets output in the 2040s, by which point a world on a 1.5 °C path has little use for it. On that reasoning a new field is not filling a gap but adding to an overshoot, and refusing it protects the investor as much as the climate, since the asset most likely to be stranded is the one sanctioned last.

The case for waiting begins from the rate at which existing fields deplete, which outruns any plausible rate of demand decline. A supply decline running ahead of a demand decline does not produce a transition; it produces price spikes, which fall hardest on low-income households, discredit climate policy and, in Europe after 2022, triggered a round of coal restarts and new liquefied gas contracts that raised emissions. On this view the sequence matters more than the destination: build the replacement, then close the licensing window. The disagreement is not really about the destination, since both sides name the same one.

questions.text: Who should cut production first, the wealthiest producers or the highest-cost ones?
questions.why: Cost says shut the most expensive barrels, which leaves cheap Gulf production running. Equity says the countries that grew rich on extraction and have the most alternatives should go first. The two principles rank countries almost in reverse.
questions.detail:
Richest-first is the framing of the treaty campaign and of the Santa Marta process, and it follows the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities written into the UN climate convention itself. The European Parliament’s April 2026 briefing notes that the Global South holds about 78 percent of world fossil fuel reserves, so a cost-ranked wind-down would ask the poorest holders to keep producing while rich countries decarbonize at home and then close the market behind them. Advocates usually pair it with payment, and point to Ecuador’s 2007 Yasuní-ITT proposal — leave the oil underground in exchange for half its value in international contributions — which raised a small fraction of its target and collapsed, as evidence that the world asks for restraint without funding it.

Costliest-first minimizes the economic loss per tonne of CO2 avoided, which means more abatement for the same money. It also tracks what markets do anyway: when demand falls, the highest-cost barrel is the one that stops, so a policy fighting that is spending political capital to make the transition more expensive. The equity ranking is also less clean than it looks. Norway’s sovereign wealth fund can absorb a phase-out, but so can Saudi Arabia’s, while Canada’s oil sands employ a region that cannot. The right instrument for fairness, on this view, is cash transfers rather than production quotas.

questions.text: Would restricting supply cause price shocks severe enough to break public support for climate policy?
questions.why: Energy price spikes have measurably moved votes since 2022, but the effect of climate policy is hard to separate from war, pandemic recovery and monetary policy. Both sides read Europe’s 2022 crisis as proof of their own case.
questions.detail:
Those who expect a breaking point point to what happened after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, when European prices for oil, coal and gas rose by roughly 40, 130 and 180 percent within two weeks, on European Central Bank analysis cited in the European Parliament’s briefing on the Santa Marta conference. The political response in Europe and North America was fuel subsidies, coal restarts and new import contracts, the opposite of a phase-out; the OECD records emergency support measures peaking at USD 163.9 billion in 2022 and still running at USD 57.7 billion in 2024. The argument is that supply restriction deliberately creates those conditions, and a policy whose first visible effect is a higher heating bill will be reversed before it bites.

Those who think the shocks are survivable note that the same crisis produced the fastest expansion of renewables and heat pumps in European history, and that the UK Climate Change Committee concluded in 2026 that reaching net zero by 2050 would cost less than the impact of a single major fossil fuel price shock. On this reading volatility is a property of fossil fuel markets rather than of climate policy: an economy that depends on imported hydrocarbons is exposed whether or not it restricts anything, and the way out is to need less of the commodity. A scheduled, announced decline is also the opposite of a shock.

questions.text: Is natural gas a bridge through the transition, or part of what must be phased out?
questions.why: Gas emits about half the CO2 of coal per unit of electricity but leaks methane across its supply chain, at rates that are genuinely uncertain. The verdict also depends on what the gas displaces: coal, or renewables plus storage.
questions.detail:
The bridge case rests on what gas does in a grid. Gas plants are the cheapest firm capacity available at scale today, and a system adding large amounts of variable wind and solar needs something to cover the still, dark weeks. The International Energy Agency’s stated-policies scenario has gas demand rising nearly 1 percent a year to 2035 before leveling off, later than oil or coal. Where gas displaces coal it cuts carbon dioxide and local air pollution immediately, and in much of Asia and Africa the alternative is new coal or no electricity. Germany and Italy both treat gas this way, which is much of why the main production-restriction alliance has stayed small.

The case for treating gas like the other two fuels is that it is not bridging to anything. Planned gas output to 2050 is higher in the 2025 Production Gap Report than in the 2023 one, which looks less like a bridge than a destination. Methane accounted for 17.9 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 on the figures cited in the European Parliament’s Santa Marta briefing, and the energy agency attributes more than 35 percent of methane emissions to fossil fuel production and use. A gas plant built in 2026 has a thirty-year life, and the capital, contracts and pipelines around it create constituencies for keeping it running. On this view bridge has functioned as a word that defers the decision indefinitely.

questions.text: Can a binding international agreement on production be negotiated, or do voluntary coalitions do more?
questions.why: Supply-side cooperation has a plausible precedent in arms control and the Montreal Protocol, and a discouraging one in every attempt to get fossil fuel language into a UN climate decision. Both sides can point to the same record.
questions.detail:
The treaty case rests on concentration. Production sits with a handful of states while consumption is spread across billions of people, so an agreement among a modest number of parties would cover most of world supply, which is true of no demand-side instrument. Non-proliferation regimes and the Montreal Protocol both worked by constraining supply among a limited set of producers, with a fund for those who could least afford it, and the world court’s 2025 opinion gives such an instrument a legal foundation it did not have before. The campaign has grown from one endorsing state in 2022 to 18 in 2026, plus 199 subnational governments and the European Parliament, which supporters read as a norm forming.

The case for coalitions answers that those 18 states produce almost nothing between them, and that at the 2025 UN climate conference more than half the parties refused even non-binding phase-out language, which is precisely why the Santa Marta track exists outside the UN process at all. An instrument requiring the consent of the countries that hold the supply will not be signed by them, and time spent pursuing it is time not spent on measures that need no unanimity: national end dates, export credit restrictions, subsidy removal, and the slower work that turned no new coal from a slogan into the default position of most rich-country governments within a decade.

questions.text: Should courts enforce limits on extraction, or should elected governments decide?
questions.why: Climate litigation has moved from a fringe tactic to a decisive one in several countries, and the world court opinion gives domestic judges new material. Whether that is the rule of law working or a political choice displaced is a question about democracy.
questions.detail:
Those who want courts involved argue that rights which exist only when a government feels like honoring them are not rights. In the United Kingdom, consents for the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields were quashed by the Court of Session in January 2025 because ministers had not assessed the emissions from burning the oil and gas, following the Supreme Court’s reasoning in the Finch case. Supporters stress what that decision did and did not do: it did not set energy policy, it required the decision to be made with the relevant facts in front of it. That is procedural discipline rather than a substantive veto, and in their view it is the ordinary function of judicial review.

Those who want the decision left to politics answer that a country’s energy prices, industrial base and fiscal position are the paradigm case of what elections are for, and that handing them to judges removes the mechanism by which a losing side consents to the outcome. They note that the same machinery runs in the other direction: arbitral tribunals have ordered governments to pay compensation for refusing extraction rights, which is also policy set by adjudication. A world in which extraction policy is settled by litigation is a world in which it is settled by whoever litigates best, and the result is neither coherent nor revisable at an election.

positions.name: Stop licensing new extraction and set national end dates
positions.steelman: The cheapest barrel never burned is the one never drilled. We seize nothing — we simply stop selling new rights to extract, and publish the date our own production ends.
positions.detail:
Every new field is a thirty-year commitment made on the assumption that the world will fail its own climate targets, and governments should stop underwriting that bet with licenses, leases and export credit. Nobody’s existing wells are taken and no contract is torn up. The state declines to sell new rights and publishes the date its production ends, so that companies, workers and regions can plan around it. Done this way the decline comes from geology rather than confiscation, since fields deplete by several percent a year on their own, and the state keeps the proceeds of its remaining output to fund the transition instead of paying arbitral awards afterward.

The arithmetic behind this is that extraction already producing or under construction commits 936 billion tonnes of CO2, well past any budget consistent with 1.5 °C, so the question is not only what gets built next. Coal is the demonstration that the method works: the Powering Past Coal Alliance grew to around 180 national, subnational and corporate members and drove the first UN climate decision ever to name a fossil fuel. Told that one country’s restraint is another’s market share, we answer that pass-through is not zero, and that licensing decisions work through expectations about future demand as much as through today’s price. The countries best placed to go first are rich ones whose public finances can absorb it, which is exactly the sequence critics say fairness requires.
positions.proponents: Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance; Government of Denmark; Government of France; Government of Costa Rica

positions.name: Cut the emissions, not the production
positions.steelman: Attack the emissions and you keep the energy. Attack the energy and you get shortage, price spikes and a backlash that costs you the emissions as well.
positions.detail:
The objective written into the UN climate convention is stabilizing greenhouse gas concentrations, not choosing which energy sources people are allowed to use. The practical path runs through carbon capture, methane abatement, efficiency and lower-carbon production techniques, all of which cut emissions per unit of energy without asking the two billion people still cooking over biomass to wait. Demand is the thing that is actually growing. An industry that stops investing while demand rises does not create a transition; it creates a crisis. Nearly 90 percent of upstream spending since 2019 has gone to offsetting the decline of existing fields rather than to growth, which makes continued investment maintenance rather than expansion, and halting it would take roughly 8 percent of world oil supply off the market every year.

Norway holds a lower-carbon version of the same position, awarding exploration acreage while taxing offshore CO2 and electrifying platforms, on the argument that its barrels are among the least emissions-intensive and that cutting them hands share to dirtier producers. Told that abatement technology has never scaled and functions as a license to delay, we answer that carbon capture has been starved of the policy support wind and solar received for two decades, and that methane abatement is not speculative at all: it is leak detection and equipment replacement, with a known cost and an immediate effect, which the EU’s 2024 Methane Regulation mandates. Restricting supply without a demonstrated replacement is also a bet on technology — one whose failure mode is a shortage rather than a missed target.
positions.proponents: OPEC; American Petroleum Institute; Government of Norway; Gas Exporting Countries Forum; Haitham Al Ghais; Mike Sommers

positions.name: Wind production down under a binding treaty
positions.steelman: Thirty years of climate agreements counted emissions at the tailpipe and never once counted the barrels at the wellhead. Only a negotiated schedule of declines closes that gap.
positions.detail:
A government can sign a net-zero pledge on Monday and award exploration blocks on Tuesday without any formal contradiction, because nothing in the climate regime measures what comes out of the ground. Production is where the problem is concentrated and where coordination is genuinely feasible: a handful of states produce most of the world’s fossil energy, while consumption is spread across billions of people who would each have to change. Arms control and the ozone treaty show that limiting what a small group of producers makes can work where limiting what everyone consumes cannot, and both came with a fund for those least able to afford the change. The instrument we want does the same — a global registry of reserves and production, a negotiated schedule of declines with the wealthiest producers moving fastest, and financing for the economies that live on extraction.

Voluntary pledges have not worked. Government production plans run 35 percent past what those same governments’ own climate pledges imply for 2030, and the 2025 accounting found the shortfall against a safe pathway wider than the 2023 one did. Told that the states holding the supply will never sign, we answer that treaties are built by a core of first movers and widened under pressure, as the Mine Ban Treaty and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons were. The function of this first phase is to build the registry, the schedule and the finance mechanism, so that the instrument exists when the political moment arrives. The alternative on offer is another decade of consensus processes that have never once named production.
positions.proponents: Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative; Government of Vanuatu; Government of Tuvalu; Government of Fiji; Government of the Marshall Islands; Government of Timor-Leste

positions.name: Keep developing reserves while wealthy producers cut first
positions.steelman: World output has to fall, but the sequence is the whole question, and a continent where hundreds of millions of people lack electricity should not be the one asked to go first.
positions.detail:
The industrial world built its wealth on coal and oil for two centuries and now proposes a rule, to take effect the moment poorer countries find their own, that nobody may do it again. Roughly four-fifths of the world’s remaining fossil fuel reserves sit in countries that contributed almost none of the historical emissions. A sequence set by cost, or by who happens to move first, keeps Norway and Texas pumping while Senegal and Uganda are told their gas is a stranded asset before it has earned anything. Where extraction revenue averages 38.6 percent of government income, surrendering it without a replacement is not an abstraction about ambition; it is schools and clinics closing. Give us the finance and the technology to leapfrog and we will use them. Until then the resources under our ground are the only development capital we have.

Energy poverty is not an abstraction either: more than 600 million Africans have no electricity and close to a billion no clean cooking, on the African Energy Chamber’s figures. Told that new African and Caribbean production will be stranded, leaving debt and no revenue, we answer that the risk is a reason for better contract terms, faster development and domestic processing, not for abstention — a country that declines to develop its reserves is guaranteed nothing at all, while one that develops them quickly captures value while the market exists. And the stranding warning is pressed hardest by institutions in countries that are still issuing licenses themselves, whose promise that the finance will arrive later has a poor record across the last decade.
positions.proponents: African Energy Chamber; Government of Guyana; Government of India; NJ Ayuk; Mohamed Irfaan Ali

positions.name: Build the replacement instead of restricting supply
positions.steelman: Nobody burns coal because a license was issued; they burn it because it is the cheapest firm power they can get. Make the substitute cheaper and extraction stops without a ban.
positions.detail:
The question as posed — restrict supply or curb demand — assumes the bottleneck is willpower. It is not. It is the price and availability of the substitute. When solar, batteries, geothermal and nuclear beat the alternative on cost and reliability, fossil fuels stop coming out of the ground without anyone passing a law, and where they do not, a prohibition produces either a shortage or a workaround. The fossil share of world energy barely moved in thirty-five years, and not because licensing was too easy: the replacement was not ready or cheap enough across heat, heavy industry, shipping and firm power. Put the effort where the leverage is — clean firm generation, industrial heat, cement and steel, grid build-out, and permitting reform for the new thing rather than prohibition of the old.

Clean energy investment reached about USD 2.2 trillion in 2026 against roughly USD 1.2 trillion for oil, gas and coal, a two-to-one ratio achieved by cost rather than by prohibition, and solar costs fell about 80 percent between 2014 and 2024 on the energy agency figures cited in the European Parliament’s briefing. Told that waiting for technology is the oldest delay tactic there is, we answer that we are not asking anyone to wait; we are asking that money and political attention go to deployment and to the hard sectors instead of to licensing fights, and we have backed nuclear, geothermal and industrial decarbonization that much of the climate movement ignored. We concede the strongest form of the objection, that cheap clean energy adds to supply unless something also pushes fossil fuels out, and our answer is a carbon price and sector standards applied at the point of use.
positions.proponents: Clean Air Task Force; Breakthrough Energy; Bill Gates

crux.lead: Is the world’s fossil fuel problem a supply problem or a demand problem?
crux.lead_highlight: a supply problem or a demand problem
crux.subtitle: Almost everyone in this argument accepts that emissions have to fall. They split over which end of the system is holding that up: how easy it still is to dig the fuels out, or how little else does the job at the price.
crux.empirical: Much of this is measurable. When one country leaves fuel in the ground, how much of it stays unburned rather than surfacing somewhere else, and does the answer differ between fuels that travel the world and fuels that do not? How much idle capacity can respond, and how fast? Does refusing permission change what investors expect, as distinct from what gets pumped in the near term? The ranges stay wide because the policy has barely been tried.
crux.values: The rest is a choice about who pays. If production has to fall, somebody’s wells close first, and whether that is settled by cost, by wealth and historical responsibility, or by who happens to hold a permit is a judgment about fairness. So is the weight given to a cost that is certain and near — higher bills, closed mines, a region without an industry — against a harm that is probable, distant and falls largely on people who cannot vote on it.

actions.title: Production Gap Report 2025
actions.description: The annual accounting of what governments plan to extract, rather than what they pledge to emit, with country profiles of the 20 largest producers. The primary document behind most figures in this debate.

actions.title: Carbon Brief on the Santa Marta conference
actions.description: A detailed, sourced account of the April 2026 conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels: what it produced, what it did not, and who turned up.

actions.title: Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance declaration and membership
actions.description: The text core members sign, ending new licensing and setting a dated end point for production, with the list of national and subnational members, which as of 2026 included none of the top oil and gas producers.
actions.for_position: Stop licensing new extraction and set national end dates

actions.title: OPEC on investment and the energy mix
actions.description: The producers’ case in their own words: demand projections to 2050, the investment they say meeting it requires, and the argument that policy should target emissions rather than energy sources.
actions.for_position: Cut the emissions, not the production

actions.title: Endorse or lobby for a fossil fuel treaty
actions.description: The campaign for a binding international instrument on production. The site lets individuals, organizations, cities and parliamentarians add an endorsement, and supplies model motions for local councils.
actions.for_position: Wind production down under a binding treaty

actions.title: African Energy Chamber
actions.description: The main advocacy body for African oil and gas development, arguing that energy access and industrialization come first and that restriction falls hardest on countries with the least historical responsibility.
actions.for_position: Keep developing reserves while wealthy producers cut first

actions.title: Clean Air Task Force
actions.description: A climate organization working on the technologies the transition needs in hard sectors — advanced nuclear, superhot rock geothermal, carbon capture, zero-carbon fuels — rather than on restricting extraction.
actions.for_position: Build the replacement instead of restricting supply

actions.title: The world court’s climate advisory opinion
actions.description: The Court’s case page for the unanimous July 2025 opinion, with the full text, the summary and the separate declarations. Paragraph 427 is the passage on production, licensing and subsidies.

actions.title: Global Energy Monitor project trackers
actions.description: Open, project-level databases of coal plants and mines, oil and gas fields, pipelines and export terminals worldwide, searchable by country, so you can see what is proposed near you and who is building it.

actions.title: Coalition on Phasing Out Fossil Fuel Incentives Including Subsidies
actions.description: An intergovernmental coalition whose members commit to publish a national inventory of fossil fuel subsidies within a year of joining. The member list is the place to check whether your government has signed up.
actions.for_position: Stop licensing new extraction and set national end dates
